title: Standard MCQ pool
note: Built by scripts/mcq-pool.mjs: candidates from the stations, generate-mcq.mjs, the open USMLE-style banks in data/benchmarks and student submissions, admitted on the flaw checks, the model review and the bars calibrated on the benchmarks (docs/mcq.md). provenance.kind says where each came from: user, ai, amsa or usmle-resource.

questions.stem:
Two weeks after undergoing an emergency cardiac catherization with stenting for unstable angina pectoris, a 61-year-old man has decreased urinary output and malaise. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and osteoarthritis of the hips. Prior to admission, his medications were insulin and naproxen. He was also started on aspirin, clopidogrel, and metoprolol after the coronary intervention. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 93/min, and blood pressure is 125/85 mm Hg. Examination shows mottled, reticulated purplish discoloration of the feet. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin count 14 g/dL
Leukocyte count 16,400/mm3
Segmented neutrophils 56%
Eosinophils 11%
Lymphocytes 31%
Monocytes 2%
Platelet count 260,000/mm3
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/h
Serum
Urea nitrogen 25 mg/dL
Creatinine 4.2 mg/dL
Renal biopsy shows intravascular spindle-shaped vacuoles. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?"

source.name: MedQA (Jin et al. 2020), US, 4-option, test split

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman in the emergency department. She woke 6 hours ago with central pressure going to the left shoulder and jaw, with sweating and nausea, and has 2 mm ST elevation in V2 to V5 with hs-troponin rising from 210 to 480 ng/L.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Treat ST elevation in contiguous leads with chest pain and a rising troponin as STEMI: activate the cath lab at once, with first medical contact to reperfusion within 90 minutes.
why: She has no leg pain or swelling, no previous clots, no cancer, surgery, travel or oestrogen, and the right lower lobe consolidation already explains her hypoxia and pleuritic pain.
It cannot be accepted until angiography shows no culprit lesion, and she has hypertension and a 15 pack-year smoking history that put her at risk of coronary disease.
The ST elevation is territorial in V2 to V5, which points to coronary occlusion rather than global ischaemia from demand.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man in general practice. HBsAg and total anti-HBc positive with IgM negative and anti-HBs 3, HBV DNA 850 IU/mL, born in Vietnam and his mother has hepatitis B.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Before anti-TNF therapy, screen for latent TB, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV and varicella immunity, because TNF blockade can reactivate TB and hepatitis B.
why: IgM anti-HBc negative, he feels well without jaundice, and the ALT is only mildly raised with normal bilirubin and INR.
HBsAg is positive, confirmed by neutralisation, and HBV DNA is detectable at 850 IU/mL.
Anti-HBs is only 3 mIU/mL and anti-HBc is positive, which vaccination does not cause.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old baby boy in the emergency department. A first-born 5-week-old boy whose forceful, non-bilious vomiting is getting worse and who is hungry straight after vomiting; his father had infant surgery; he has a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; ultrasound shows a 5 mm wall and a 19 mm channel.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pyloric stenosis causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
why: The vomit has never been green, lactate is normal and the superior mesenteric vein lies to the right of the artery, although this does not exclude it.
Afebrile, normal lactate, hungry and feeding keenly, and quick recovery after one fluid bolus.
Potassium is low (3.0), sodium is low-normal (134) and he has an alkalosis, not the low sodium, high potassium and acidosis of salt wasting.

questions.stem: A 28-month-old baby in general practice. Choked on mixed nuts at age 2 with the cough starting that evening, then one-sided monophonic wheeze, tracheal shift and right lower lobe collapse that did not respond to antibiotics, steroids or salbutamol.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Inhaled foreign body obstructing the right lower lobe bronchus
Community-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe
questions.explanation: A toddler with persistent cough unresponsive to antibiotics, steroids and inhalers, plus focal collapse, may have an inhaled foreign body needing bronchoscopy.
why: No TB contact or travel, no night sweats, and weight steady on the 50th centile.
Afebrile and playful, the lobe has lost volume with no air bronchograms, and a week of amoxicillin did not help.
No atopy, eczema, family history or earlier wheeze, the wheeze is one-sided and monophonic, and salbutamol and prednisolone did not help.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman in the emergency department. Older woman with known gallstones and days of on-and-off colicky pain, then faeculent vomiting, distension and no flatus, with Rigler triad on X-ray and no previous biliary surgery to explain the pneumobilia.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Gallstone ileus causing small bowel obstruction
questions.explanation: Murphy's sign is elicited by palpating under the right costal margin while the patient breathes in; inspiratory arrest suggests acute cholecystitis.
why: No fever, jaundice or confusion, and bilirubin and ALP are normal, so she has only one part of Charcot triad.
Lactate is normal at 1.8 and the pain is colicky rather than constant, although neither rules it out.
Murphy's sign is negative, she is afebrile, the pain comes and goes, and the main problem is mechanical small bowel obstruction.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man in clinic. His reactive fourth-generation screen was confirmed on Western blot and on a second sample, he had a negative test 14 months ago, a seroconversion-type illness 2 months ago and a high viral load of 86,000 copies/mL.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: False-positive HIV screening test or sample labelling error
HIV-2 infection or HIV-1 and HIV-2 dual infection
questions.explanation: HIV mainly infects CD4 helper T cells; progressive CD4 loss without treatment leads to immune failure (AIDS).
why: His CD4 is above 200 and above 14%, he has no weight loss, fevers, cough, oral candida or other AIDS-defining illness, and he had a negative test 14 months ago.
The Western blot is positive for envelope, core and polymerase antibodies, a second separately collected sample is reactive again, and the viral load is detectable.
HIV-2 antibody was not detected, and the HIV-1 Western blot and HIV-1 viral load are positive.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman in general practice. Left hearing loss came on suddenly on waking within 72 hours, with Weber to the right, Rinne positive on both sides, no air-bone gap and a loss 35 to 50 dB worse than the right over five contiguous frequencies.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is time-critical: confirm with an audiogram, start steroids promptly (oral, or intratympanic via ENT, dose per local guideline) and involve ENT the same day.
why: Her cranial nerves are normal and she has had no previous hearing problems, but only MRI of the internal auditory canals can exclude it.
She has no facial, limb, speech, swallowing or visual symptoms, her cranial nerves and coordination are normal, and the unsteadiness has settled.
Otoscopy is normal, both tympanograms are type A, there is no air-bone gap and the Weber goes to the right ear.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman in clinic. The NIPT was valid with a 9% fetal fraction and showed high chance for trisomy 16 only, while the pregnancy is ongoing and the 12-week scan was normal (NT 1.6 mm, no structural abnormality).
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Vanishing twin as the source of the trisomic cell-free DNA
questions.explanation: NIPT is a screening test on cell-free DNA in maternal blood, most of which comes from the placenta; a high-chance result is not a diagnosis and needs confirmation by CVS or amniocentesis before any decision.
why: The 12-week scan was structurally normal with a normal nuchal translucency and nasal bone present.
The fetus is alive and structurally normal at 12 weeks 1 day, with a heart rate of 158 bpm and no bleeding or pain, whereas full trisomy 16 almost always ends in early miscarriage.
The scan showed a single gestational sac with no second sac, she conceived naturally, and she has had no bleeding in this pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man in general practice. Repeated clinic readings of 150 to 154/92 to 94 mmHg in both arms, a home average of 124/78 mmHg, he says his pressure always goes up at the doctor, and there is no end-organ damage.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Drug or substance-induced raised blood pressure
questions.explanation: Raised clinic BP with normal home readings suggests white coat hypertension: confirm with ABPM or a structured home protocol before diagnosing or treating.
why: Normal potassium, eGFR above 90 with a normal urine albumin to creatinine ratio, no episodes of sweating, palpitations and headache, and equal readings in both arms.
His home readings average 124/78 mmHg, although they were taken unreliably.
His ibuprofen use is intermittent and he takes no decongestants, licorice or supplements.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in general practice. Biopsy shows Gleason 4+3=7 in 4 of 14 left cores, with PSA 9.4, a PI-RADS 4 lesion and no spread on MRI.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Metastatic or locally advanced prostate cancer
questions.explanation: PSA is organ-specific, not cancer-specific. It rises with age, BPH, prostatitis or infection and ejaculation.
why: He has no bone pain, weight loss or neurological symptoms, and MRI shows no extraprostatic extension, seminal vesicle invasion, nodal disease or bone lesions.
PSA is under 10, the grade is Group 3 rather than 4 or 5, and there is no extraprostatic extension or palpable disease.
Pattern 4 predominates (about 70%), so this is 4+3 (Grade Group 3), not 3+4.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child in the emergency department. A 2-year-old with 2 days of coryza and fever to 38 °C, then a barking cough, hoarse cry and inspiratory stridor from 8 pm, with a sibling who had a cold.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Moderate croup: a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (1.8 mg for 12 kg) or prednisolone 1 mg/kg (12 mg); severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, maximum 12 mg (7.2 mg for 12 kg).
why: Fully immunised including Hib, no drooling, swallowing normally, not toxic, and the illness began with coryza and a barking cough.
Only low-grade fever (38 °C at home, 37.8 °C on arrival), the child is alert and not toxic, and no poor response to adrenaline has been shown.
No choking episode, no small toys or food missing, and the onset was gradual after 2 days of coryza and fever.

questions.stem: A 0.6-day-old baby on the ward. Mother was GBS positive with only 2 hours of antibiotics before birth, membranes ruptured 20 hours and a fever of 38.2 °C in labour; the baby has a fever of 38.1 °C, grunting, HR 188, CRT 4 s, lactate 4.2, neutropenia with toxic changes and bilateral hazy opacification on chest X-ray.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Treat suspected early-onset sepsis urgently: blood culture, then benzylpenicillin and gentamicin (RCH Neonatal antimicrobial guidelines, doses from the Australasian Neonatal Medicines Formulary), without delaying treatment.
why: Heart size and shape are normal and the baby improved with fluid and oxygen, but this does not exclude it, so pre- and post-ductal SpO2 are needed.
BGL and electrolytes are normal, there is a fever, and poor perfusion explains the lactate; check ammonia if not improving.
Fever, shock and neutropenia, onset after 10 hours of normal feeding, and no fluid in the fissures on the chest X-ray.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 4-month-old baby in the emergency department. First episode at 4 months with 3 days of coryza then cough, RR 64, recession, widespread fine crackles and wheeze, low-grade fever and a sibling with a cold.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Start oxygen when SpO2 is persistently below 90% in room air, and target 90% or above.
why: Well newborn period with no known heart problems, CRT 2 seconds, and the liver edge is pushed down by hyperinflation rather than enlarged.
Alert and making eye contact, CRT 2 seconds, BP 90/55, only low-grade fever and BGL 5.2 mmol/L.
No apnoea, colour change or coughing paroxysms, and immunised including the 4-month vaccines.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 27-month-old baby in the emergency department. A single generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 3 minutes in a febrile 27-month-old with a viral URTI, back to GCS 15 within an hour and a sibling who had a febrile seizure.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A simple febrile seizure is generalised tonic-clonic, under 15 minutes, with complete recovery within 1 hour and no recurrence in the same illness.
why: No neck stiffness, rash, vomiting or recent antibiotics, a clear URTI source, and alert with GCS 15 and a normal neurological exam by 18:55.
BGL was 5.6 mmol/L at triage and the child recovered fully without glucose.
No focal onset or one-sided features, it lasted about 3 minutes, there was no repeat and recovery was complete within the hour.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man in the emergency department. An hour of central crushing pain to the left jaw with sweating and nausea, hypertension, untreated high cholesterol and premature family history, ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL, a raised troponin, and new bradycardia with hypotension.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute aortic dissection extending into the right coronary artery
questions.explanation: STEMI is an ECG and clinical diagnosis. Activate the cath lab without waiting for the troponin, aiming for primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact.
why: The pain came on gradually as a pressure, it is not tearing and does not go to the back, the arm BPs and pulses are equal, and there is no aortic regurgitation murmur.
No immobility, surgery, cancer or calf symptoms, the pain is not pleuritic, SpO2 is 97% on room air and the calves are normal.
No viral prodrome, the pain is pressure-like and not positional, there is no rub, and the ST elevation is territorial with reciprocal depression in aVL.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in general practice. Age 75 with asbestos exposure in the late 1960s and 1970s, progressive dry cough and exertional breathlessness, 6 kg weight loss, hoarseness, dull upper right chest pain, right apical dullness and a 6 cm right apical mass on the chest X-ray.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Primary lung carcinoma of the right superior sulcus
questions.explanation: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with weight loss, hoarseness, chest pain or breathlessness in an older adult needs a chest X-ray. A suspicious film needs an urgent CT and specialist referral, with the patient seen within 2 weeks.
why: The X-ray shows a discrete apical mass with no pleural effusion, plaques or pleural thickening.
No fevers, night sweats, travel or TB contact, and the lesion is a solid mass without cavitation.
No clubbing, no fine crackles, no reticular change on the X-ray, and it does not explain the mass.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman in general practice. Two spontaneous attacks of spinning vertigo lasting about 8 hours, fluctuating right hearing loss with tinnitus and fullness, a documented right low-frequency sensorineural loss, and a normal examination between attacks.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ménière's disease of the right ear
questions.explanation: Clarify what “dizzy” means first. True vertigo is vestibular, and its timing and triggers (seconds and positional, hours and spontaneous, or days and continuous) narrow the cause.
why: The symptoms are episodic and the loss is low-frequency, with good word recognition, present acoustic reflexes and normal cranial nerves V and VII.
The attacks lasted 8 hours each with full recovery, there are no neurological symptoms, the examination is normal and the ear symptoms point to the inner ear.
No headache, aura or light or noise sensitivity, and she has a documented one-sided low-frequency sensorineural loss.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman in general practice. Diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, exophthalmos and lid retraction, weight loss, tremor, warm moist hands, AF, suppressed TSH with high free T4 and T3, and positive TRAb.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Examine thyroid status as well as the gland: hands, tremor, reflexes, eyes from the front, side and above, the neck with a swallow and tongue protrusion, palpation from behind, percussion of the manubrium, a bruit, and the legs.
why: Afebrile (37.0 °C), alert and oriented, no vomiting, only mildly increased bowel frequency, no heart failure, haemodynamically stable. A Burch–Wartofsky score may reach the mid-20s to 30s from the AF and restlessness alone, but clinically she is compensated. Admit if fever, confusion, vomiting, worsening tachycardia or heart failure develop.
She is 32, the gland is smooth and diffuse with no nodules, she has eye signs, and TRAb is positive.
There is no solitary nodule, both lobes are enlarged, and TRAb is positive.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman in the emergency department. Colicky periumbilical pain, faeculent vomiting, no stool or flatus, distension, tinkling bowel sounds, previous laparoscopy, and a CT transition point under the right iliac fossa port site with no mass or hernia.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation (no stool or flatus) are the cardinal features of bowel obstruction. Always ask specifically about flatus and previous surgery.
why: Lactate is normal, bowel wall enhancement is normal, the SMA and SMV are patent, she has no AF and the pain is colicky, not constant.
She had only one episode of diarrhoea and nothing since, she is afebrile, and the colon is collapsed on CT with no wall thickening.
Vomiting began within hours of the pain, and CT shows a collapsed colon with the transition point in the small bowel.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman in the emergency department. Sharp retrosternal pleuritic pain that is worse lying down and better sitting forward, a friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression, a febrile son 10 days ago, temperature 37.8 °C and CRP 46.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: ST-elevation myocardial infarction or other acute coronary syndrome
questions.explanation: Pericarditis pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional: worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward. Acute pericarditis needs 2 of 4 criteria: typical pain, a friction rub, typical ECG changes and a pericardial effusion.
why: She is 34 with no cardiovascular risk factors, the pain is sharp, pleuritic and positional, the ST elevation spans limb and chest leads without fitting one coronary territory, with PR depression and no Q waves, and hs-troponin is normal at 0 and 2 hours.
The pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the mediastinum is not widened on the chest X-ray.
She has no breathlessness, haemoptysis, calf symptoms, previous clot, immobility or oestrogen, SpO2 is 99%, Wells is 1.5 and the D-dimer is normal.

source.name: AMSA MedEd OSCEs: Chest Pain History 2

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman in general practice. Progressive breathlessness now at 5 m with orthopnoea and PND, NSTEMI 6 months ago and hypertension, raised JVP, S3, displaced apex, bibasal crackles and effusions, 3 kg weight gain, cardiomegaly with batwing oedema on X-ray and BNP 1,280.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Recurrent myocardial ischaemia or acute coronary syndrome
Aortic stenosis or other valvular heart disease
questions.explanation: Quantify breathlessness by what the patient can do (distance, stairs, dressing), not a score out of 10. This gives the NYHA class and the impact on daily life.
why: No chest pain, sweating or nausea and no new change on the ECG; troponin is still needed.
Gradual 2-month course with orthopnoea and PND, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis or calf signs, and an X-ray that explains the picture.
No exertional syncope or chest pain, no murmur and a normal carotid upstroke; the echo will confirm.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in general practice. Six-week progressive productive cough with 5 days of haemoptysis, low-grade fever, fatigue, breathlessness and 5 kg weight loss; born in and travels annually to Cambodia; right upper zone crackles and right upper lobe opacification.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks with haemoptysis, fever and weight loss in someone born in or travelling to a country with high TB rates is pulmonary TB until proven otherwise.
why: Aged 26 with only 1.5 pack-years and a 6-week history, no clubbing or lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar enlargement on the X-ray.
Gradual productive cough with fever, no pleuritic pain, no immobility or calf signs, SpO2 97% and a normal heart rate.
No diabetes, heavy alcohol use or kidney disease; sputum culture with the lab alerted to Burkholderia will help exclude it.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man in general practice. Constant dull periumbilical pain for 12 hours with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever, pain on coughing and movement, and right iliac fossa tenderness with rebound and a positive Rovsing's sign.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Early appendicitis causes vague, constant periumbilical pain (visceral afferents) that later localises to the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
why: Lower abdominal and periumbilical rather than epigastric pain, no back radiation, and no gallstones.
No distension, bowel sounds present, and no previous abdominal surgery.
No weight loss, fatigue, diarrhoea or blood in the stool, and only a 12-hour history.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman in general practice. Two months of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, perianal inflammation with skin tags, clubbing, a smoker, calprotectin 820, and cobblestoning with skip lesions and granulomas at colonoscopy.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic diarrhoea with blood, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss or fever is organic until proven otherwise; ask about each directly, along with NSAIDs, smoking and a family history of IBD.
why: The granulomas are non-caseating, the acid-fast bacilli stain is negative, and she has no TB risk factors.
Right iliac fossa pain, perianal skin tags, terminal ileal disease, skip lesions with rectal sparing, and granulomas on biopsy.
Symptoms for 2 months with no travel, antibiotics or sick contacts, and negative stool PCR, culture and C. difficile toxin.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man in the emergency department. About 4 beers a night with 12 last night, constant epigastric pain through to the back eased by leaning forward, lipase 1850 U/L, a bulky pancreas with peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound, no gallstones and an isolated raised GGT.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ruptured or leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm
questions.explanation: Acute pancreatitis needs 2 of 3 criteria: typical epigastric pain through to the back, lipase more than 3 times the upper limit, and characteristic imaging. The height of the lipase does not reflect severity.
why: No NSAIDs or previous indigestion, no rigidity or rebound, and the lipase is more than 30 times the upper limit.
The pain is not tearing, BP is normal and equal in both arms, there is no pulsatile mass, the aorta measures 2.0 cm on ultrasound, and (partly) at 56 he is below the usual risk age.
No chest pain or breathlessness, the pain is positional, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST or T wave changes.

source.name: AMSA MedEd OSCEs: Abdominal Pain History 5

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman in the emergency department. Constant right upper quadrant pain for about 20 hours after a rich meal, radiating to the shoulder tip, with fever, chills, vomiting, earlier postprandial episodes, a positive Murphy's sign, WCC 15.8, CRP 142 and an ultrasound showing a 6 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and an impacted neck stone.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Biliary colic settles within a few hours. Constant RUQ pain lasting longer, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP, is acute cholecystitis.
why: No jaundice or confusion, bilirubin 16, common bile duct 4 mm with no duct stone, normal BP and lactate.
Pain maximal in the RUQ with only mild epigastric tenderness, no reflux or melaena, no rigidity or generalised peritonism, and the ultrasound shows a clear biliary cause.
She takes the pill daily, had a normal period 2 weeks ago, has no bleeding or faintness, a normal BP and a serum beta-hCG below 2 IU/L.

source.name: AMSA MedEd OSCEs: Abdominal Pain History 6

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman in the emergency department. She has 4 weeks of burning retrosternal pain that is worse lying down and after meals, with acid regurgitation, no exertional features, a normal ECG and negative serial troponin.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome or unstable angina
questions.explanation: In ED chest pain, rule out ACS before settling on reflux: a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, then serial high-sensitivity troponin on a validated assay-specific 0/1 h or 0/2 h pathway. A normal ECG alone does not exclude ACS.
why: The pain is burning, positional and related to meals, never exertional and has no associated features, and her ECG during pain and her troponin at 0 and 2 hours are normal.
She has no anaemia, haematemesis, hoarseness or palpable lymph nodes, and she is 45 and a non-smoker.
The pain is retrosternal rather than epigastric, with no bloating, early satiety, NSAID use or bleeding, and her Hb is normal.

source.name: AMSA MedEd OSCEs: Chest Pain History 4

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman in general practice. Jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever, confusion and hypotension with known gallstones, a cholestatic LFT pattern and a dilated duct with a distal stone.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pancreatic head carcinoma causing malignant biliary obstruction
questions.explanation: Charcot's triad (jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, fever) suggests acute cholangitis. Adding confusion and hypotension makes Reynolds' pentad, which marks sepsis with organ dysfunction and hypoperfusion and needs urgent drainage of the bile duct.
why: No weight loss or steatorrhoea, acute febrile onset, a stone seen in the duct, and no distal duct stricture or mass effect on the ERCP cholangiogram.
Normal lipase and no peripancreatic fluid on ultrasound.
Murphy's sign negative, no gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, and conjugated jaundice with a dilated common bile duct.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man in the emergency department. Sudden racing palpitations at rest for 40 minutes that he cannot tap out, an irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit, and an ECG with absent P waves, fibrillatory waves and irregular RR intervals at about 132.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pin down the exact time of onset of palpitations: under 48 hours allows early cardioversion once anticoagulation has started, while 48 hours or more (or unknown) needs a TOE or 3 to 4 weeks of anticoagulation first. Newer guidance (ESC 2024) uses 24 hours; Philip, at under 2 hours, is within both.
why: Discomfort that is not crushing or radiating, no sweating or nausea, no ischaemic ST change and a normal 0-hour hs-troponin, which still needs repeating.
No sawtooth flutter waves, and the RR intervals are irregular with no repeating pattern.
No weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, goitre or eye signs, with a normal TSH and free T4.

eval.judge: claude-opus-5-5 via the Claude Code CLI

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man in general practice. Four months of daily burning retrosternal pain after dinner, worse lying down and with spicy food, with an acid taste in the throat, a night cough and a normal ECG and bloods.
questions.ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying down, with an acid taste and a night cough, is typical of GORD, which is a clinical diagnosis.
why: No dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting or anaemia, and a short 4-month history.
